title: Trends and research foci of robotics-based STEM education: a systematic review from diverse angles based on the technology-based learning model
extended_summary:
This paper asks what the existing research on robotics-based STEM (R-STEM) education shows across three dimensions: research characteristics, participant-robot interaction, and how robotics is used in STEM instruction. The authors argue that prior reviews had not fully captured the role of robotics in STEM learning, especially in terms of disciplinary integration, educational goals, and the kinds of learners and teachers involved.

To address this gap, the paper systematically reviews 39 SSCI journal articles published from 2012 to 2021 and indexed in Web of Science. The reviewed studies covered K-12 and some higher education settings, with many conducted in the United States and a large share involving elementary students. Across the studies, robots were most often used as learning tools, most commonly LEGO MINDSTORMS, and the dominant STEM focus was technology, especially programming. The most frequent instructional approach was project-based learning.

The review concludes that R-STEM research has largely emphasized learner and teacher perceptions, learning performance, and motivational outcomes rather than rigorous evidence on long-term achievement. It also finds that science and mathematics are less represented than technology and engineering, and that most studies use robots to support content integration rather than as intelligent tutors. The authors recommend more research on low-cost robotics, stronger pedagogical design, broader disciplinary balance, and greater attention to teachers and higher education contexts.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review with transparent search and coding procedures, but it is not a meta-analysis and does not estimate pooled causal effects. The evidence base summarized is largely descriptive and heterogeneous, so credibility for effect estimation is limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests generally positive but mixed impacts of robotics on learning, motivation, and durable skills, yet no pooled effect sizes are reported. Because the paper is syntheses-of-syntheses and the underlying evidence is mixed, the practical impact is promising but unclear in magnitude.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of robotics-based STEM education, focusing on physical educational robots (especially LEGO MINDSTORMS and Arduino-based kits) used as learning tools, tutees, or occasional tutors in K-12 STEM instruction.

finding.finding_summary: This review synthesized 39 studies of robotics-based STEM education rather than estimating a single pooled effect. Across the literature, robotics was most often linked to learning performance and conceptual understanding in programming/technology and STEM problem-solving, but the evidence was mixed: for learning performance, 6 studies reported positive effects, 2 found no significant difference, and 5 found mixed or conditional results.
finding.measure: Learning performance; conceptual understanding in STEM/programming tasks
finding.study_size: n=39 studies (with learning performance measured in 15 studies)

finding.finding_summary: The review found that affective outcomes were a major focus: 23 of 39 studies examined perceptions, attitudes, motivation, self-efficacy, interest, or satisfaction. Of these, 14 studies reported positive perceptions of robotics in STEM, while 9 reported mixed results, suggesting generally favorable but not uniform motivational/attitudinal effects.
finding.measure: Technology acceptance, attitude and motivation, self-efficacy, satisfaction/interest, learning perceptions

finding.finding_summary: Robotics-based STEM was frequently used to support durable skills such as problem-solving, collaboration/teamwork, communication, creativity, and higher-order thinking. The review reports that problem-solving (6 studies), communication (8), collaboration/teamwork (4), and creativity (4) were commonly targeted, with several studies reporting positive results and few negative findings.
finding.measure: Problem-solving, collaboration/teamwork, communication, creativity, critical thinking, higher-order thinking

finding.finding_summary: A smaller subset of studies examined operational or psychomotor skills such as construction, building, and modeling robots. The review states that 3 of 5 studies found positive results, indicating that robotics activities can improve hands-on technical execution and build-related task performance.
